items.title: Big Tech Q3 2026 earnings — overnight update: sell-side analysts put specific 2027 numbers on Meta's 'notably larger' framing (Wedbush $249B, Morgan Stanley $225B, both up materially from prior ~$210B), and Apple's Nov 2 consensus comes in ABOVE Apple's own $111.7–$113.7B guide at $115.06–$115.33B revenue / $2.01–$2.02 EPS, which raises the bar going into Monday's call
items.summary: The four hyperscaler Q3 2026 prints are in and the Oct 31 enrichment captured the full four-print picture: Microsoft (Oct 28 after close) printed $92.3B revenue (+19%), Azure $33.2B (+48%, first-time dollar disclosure above its ~45% guide), Microsoft Cloud $63.9B (+30%), net income $36.6B (+32%), capex $39.4B BELOW the ~$50B expected on a $175B calendar-2026 capex guide held unchanged, shares ~+8% after hours; Alphabet (Oct 28) printed $127.6B revenue (+25%), Google Cloud $30.7B (+103%), Cloud operating margin 23.7%→36.2%, capex $51.4B producing ~−$9.1B FCF, EPS $2.12 missed ~$3.00 consensus, shares ~−8%; Meta (Oct 29) printed $64.6B revenue vs $63.3B expected but GAAP EPS $3.83 vs $6.67 on a $9.89B litigation charge, Q3 capex $34.9B with −$2.12B FCF, 2026 capex narrowed to $135–145B, 'notably larger' AI investments in 2027; Amazon (Oct 29) reported AWS $46B (+39%, fastest in 18 quarters), AWS operating income $17.8B at 38.7% margin, AWS backlog $578B with triple-digit YoY growth, Jassy guides AWS >40% in 2027 and 2028, overall EPS $1.89 vs ~$1.96, Q4 revenue guide $240–247B below estimates, trailing FCF ~−$42.4B, shares −6% to −9%. Combined four-hyperscaler calendar-2026 capex total of roughly $720B, up from ~$410B in 2025. Overnight additions since Oct 31 11:55Z refresh: (1) Wedbush raised its 2027 Meta capex estimate from $210B to $249B specifically citing compute needed for Meta's Muse AI products, which is the first concrete sell-side number put on Zuckerberg's 'notably larger' 2027 framing; Morgan Stanley separately lifted its 2027 estimate to about $225B (~29% above its prior work); Needham's Laura Martin advised investors to 'stay on the sidelines' on Meta, pointing to the stated 'hundreds of billions of dollars' AI investment path. (2) Apple's Monday Nov 2 consensus has firmed up: Chartmill shows $115.33B revenue / $2.02 EPS, FXEmpire shows $115.06B / $2.01 EPS (27 analysts), ChartRow shows $1.98 EPS across 8 analysts — the revenue consensus is roughly $1.3–$3.6B ABOVE the top of Apple's own $111.7–$113.7B guide, so the bar going into Monday is specifically higher than Apple's print would need to clear its own framing.
items.why_it_matters: The overnight window sharpens two specific things that weren't quantified yet in yesterday's am. First, 'notably larger' in 2027 now has sell-side numbers attached — Wedbush at $249B and Morgan Stanley at ~$225B both land materially above the prior ~$210B baseline, and both tie the increase to the Muse AI product line rather than a generic data-center buildout, which means the January call will be the specific test of whether Meta tries to pull those numbers back down. If Meta walks them back, that's the capex-discipline framing from the Oct 30 pm playing out exactly as hypothesized. If Meta doesn't, the sell-side is now anchored to a 2027 number that pencils out to another ~40–50% YoY capex increase from the $135–145B 2026 range, which would be the single clearest signal that this cycle is being underwritten on faith in a 2028+ demand curve rather than a 2026–2027 revenue curve. Second, Apple's Monday consensus comes in above Apple's own guide — Chartmill $115.33B revenue / $2.02 EPS and FXEmpire $115.06B / $2.01 EPS versus Apple's $111.7–$113.7B guide. This is diagnostic because Apple is the one Big Tech name where capex is NOT the central narrative — the question on this call is whether iPhone 18 Pro launch-week sales and Siri AI (English, iOS 27, September 14 rollout) show up in the top-line or in Services. If Apple just meets its own guide and misses the sell-side consensus, the stock reaction will tell you how much of the AI premium is already priced in; if Apple beats consensus, that's the clearest datum we'll get on whether on-device AI drives upgrade cycles the way the Oct 30 pm digest hypothesized. For a hobbyist Python coder, the overnight additions tighten three practical items: (1) if Meta's 2027 does walk back in January, that signals the broader AI-API price floor isn't going down nearly as fast as the raw compute buildout implies, because the LLM providers need to pay for the compute somehow; (2) the Apple print is the one most likely to directly change what shows up in iOS developer previews — Siri AI functionality that ships in revenue is Siri AI functionality that gets more engineering investment next year; (3) the Microsoft-rewarded-for-capex-discipline framing stays intact and is the single clearest signal that developer-tier Azure OpenAI pricing is less likely to rise over 2027 than Google Cloud or AWS pricing is. Specific numbers to watch over the next 48 hours: (a) Apple's Nov 2 at 2:00 PM PT revenue print against both the $111.7–$113.7B guide and the $115.06–$115.33B consensus; (b) any explicit Nov 2 Apple guidance on fiscal Q1 2027 iPhone revenue growth (prior guide was 9–11% YoY for Q4; Q1 includes the full post-launch iPhone 18 Pro quarter); (c) whether the stock reaction mirrors Microsoft's (reward for guide-under-expected) or follows the Alphabet/Meta/Amazon pattern (punishment for guide-under-consensus).

items.title: OpenAI reportedly plans to buy Google TPUs — overnight update: two new secondary signals (Alphabet CFO reportedly said most TPU-sales revenue would show up in 2027; Google Cloud's Thomas Kurian said customers should have 'a broad selection of models, including those from OpenAI') line up with the original scoop but still fall short of primary confirmation
items.summary: The Information reported on October 27, 2026 that OpenAI is preparing to purchase Google TPU chips rather than only renting TPU capacity through Google Cloud, and Reuters plus Bloomberg relayed the same reporting through Oct 27–28. The Oct 31 enrichment noted that Alphabet's Oct 28 Q3 2026 earnings call did not call out an OpenAI-specific TPU customer by name, which was a datum but not a disconfirmation. The overnight window (Oct 31 17:15Z → Nov 1 06:00Z) adds two further secondary signals that line up with the original scoop while still falling short of primary confirmation: (1) Alphabet's CFO reportedly warned that most revenue from TPU sales agreements is likely to show up in 2027 rather than immediately — a framing that explains why Alphabet would not have called out a specific TPU customer on an Oct 28 call even if a purchase were agreed; (2) Google Cloud's Thomas Kurian is quoted saying the company wants customers to have 'a broad selection of models, including those from OpenAI,' which pattern-matches a reciprocal commercial arrangement without confirming its scope. OpenAI already announced last week that it would make its frontier models available through Google Cloud, which is adjacent to but distinct from the TPU-purchase story. Supporting evidence from the original reporting still stands: OpenAI has posted job listings for engineers to tune its models for TPU hardware; OpenAI began using rented Google TPU capacity in mid-2025; TrendForce separately reports Oracle plans to bring TPUs into its cloud offering in 2027. Volume, price, and timeline for an OpenAI–Google TPU purchase remain not disclosed, and the single-anonymous-source nature of the original scoop remains the main caveat.
items.why_it_matters: The overnight additions sharpen the Oct 31 enrichment's point rather than contradicting it. The Oct 31 framing — 'Alphabet had the natural venue to confirm an OpenAI deal on Oct 28 and chose not to; that's not a disconfirmation, but it is a datum' — tightens one specific way: Alphabet's CFO reportedly saying most TPU-sales revenue shows up in 2027 is a straightforward reason not to call out a specific marquee customer on the Oct 28 call. Public TPU-sales commitments that only start producing revenue in 2027 would also still be disclosable under Reg FD at the point they close rather than at the point they're announced, so the absence of a name-check on Oct 28 is consistent with either (a) a deal that exists but hasn't closed, or (b) a deal that hasn't been reached. Kurian's 'broad selection of models, including those from OpenAI' quote is softer evidence — it's about Google Cloud resale of OpenAI's models, which OpenAI itself confirmed last week, not about OpenAI buying TPUs. The two stories are commercial-reciprocal in a way that makes a TPU purchase more plausible without proving it. For Gabe's Python stack, the implications step forward one notch: (1) PyTorch's XLA/TPU backend quality is the single leading indicator of whether an OpenAI–TPU deal would actually ship as working inference pipelines rather than just a purchase announcement — if the next PyTorch minor release or the next torch_xla release includes new TPU-targeted optimizations contributed by OpenAI-affiliated engineers, that would be a stronger confirmation than any secondary reporting; (2) the Oracle-TPUs-in-2027 angle still matters most for anyone building across clouds, because a TPU-tuned model called from a non-Google cloud would be the first time Google's hardware is sold outside Google Cloud at scale; (3) the engineering-reality counterweight from TechRadar remains real — rebuilding CUDA-tuned training and inference stacks for TPU hardware is routinely 6–18 months of work, so even a signed deal doesn't translate into immediate production inference. Specific items to watch over the next 4–8 weeks: (a) whether Google or OpenAI publishes a joint primary announcement; (b) whether Alphabet's Q4 2026 call in late January 2027 breaks out TPU-sales revenue growth as a disclosed line item; (c) whether Oracle makes a primary announcement of its rumored 2027 TPU cloud rollout; (d) whether a follow-up Information story adds a second source or specific terms on volume, price, or timeline.

items.title: Mistral Large 4 open weights — overnight update: Vals AI composite revised to 32nd of 44 at 48.05% (previously 35th of 48 at 48.1%), published list pricing extends to $0.14/M cached input and $4.18/M output, and license-status signals remain mixed with HuggingFace card still showing 'Coming soon' per one aggregator
items.summary: The Oct 30 pm digest put Mistral Large 4 at Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index 38 (vs 9 for Large 3; 58–59 for the frontier closed models) with the 524K-vs-claimed-1M context-window gap, and the Oct 31 enrichment added Vals AI overall index 35th of 48 at 48.1%, LMArena 112th as of Oct 13, Mistral's own-run Surge AI blind coding eval 3.74/5 (2nd of 5, behind Opus 5 at 4.22), and Mistral-hosted-API pricing $1.36/M input list with $0.68/M launch discount. Overnight: a few small refinements add detail without changing the mid-pack-not-frontier framing. (1) Vals AI's composite now shows Mistral Large 4 at 32nd of 44 at 48.05% — a slight revision from the Oct 31 reading of 35th of 48 at 48.1%, likely reflecting Vals adjusting its model set. (2) Full published pricing beyond the Oct 31 input number: cached input $0.14/M tokens and output $4.18/M tokens, which quantifies the hosted-API cost structure more completely. (3) License-status signals remain mixed — some aggregator pages still show 'Coming soon' in the Hugging Face license cell for Large 4 (vs the Oct 29 TNW article that reported the weights released), and secondary reporting is split between 'custom license' and 'near-MIT.' This does not contradict the weights being released on Oct 29 but does mean the specific license text is not fully nailed down in widely-indexed sources yet. The HuggingFace listing, the 4× B200/B300 inference hardware requirement, the ~524K vs claimed 1M practical context window, and the vLLM/SGLang Python inference path from the am and pm all remain accurate.
items.why_it_matters: The overnight refinements don't change the mid-pack framing — they tighten the numbers. The useful additions for Gabe: (1) the full hosted-API pricing ($1.36/M input list, $0.68/M launch discount, $0.14/M cached input, $4.18/M output) makes it easier to size whether the hosted API or self-hosted path is cheaper for a specific use case. For a workload that reads lots of context (RAG, long documents) with modest generation, the cached-input price at $0.14/M makes repeated-prompt scenarios ~10x cheaper than non-cached — which matters for a hobbyist Python stack where the same reference material gets passed into many calls. For a workload that generates lots of text per call (code generation, long summaries), the output price at $4.18/M dominates and the self-hosted path on rented 4× B200/B300 hardware becomes competitive at higher volumes. (2) The license uncertainty is the item most worth watching this week — Mistral promised 'near-MIT' at launch and the Oct 29 TNW article treated weights as released, but if widely-indexed HuggingFace model cards still show 'Coming soon' in the license cell, the specific commercial-use terms (whether a revenue-share threshold applies above a certain company size, as Alibaba Qwen's recent terms do) aren't fully settled in secondary sources yet. For Gabe personally, this doesn't change anything — hobbyist use is covered under essentially any plausible open-weight license — but it's the detail to confirm before building anything commercial on top. The useful framing from the pm and the Oct 31 enrichment hasn't changed: Large 4 is 'the open-weight model that's good enough to run yourself when a frontier closed-API call isn't the right tradeoff,' with best independent results in cyber reproduce-and-patch (81.7%) and Harvey Legal Agent (6th of 75 at 15.83%), and middling on the Vals general-purpose composite. The LMArena 112th ranking from Oct 13 is still the data point most likely to move in the next 2–4 weeks as users rate the open-weight version in the arena.
